ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants completed an acceptability judgement task that tested for the presence of MECs in their English Interlanguage system with a focus on the two implicational hierarchies presented above: (1) verb-type, and (2) question word.
Participants were recruited via Prolific and provided with $10 compensation for their time.
At the time of testing, participants were living in the United States (L1 English), Spain (L1 Spanish), or France (L1 French).
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old.

Participants were excluded for one or more of the following reasons: • Simultaneous bilinguals and/or English not the L2 (n = 3); • Clear lack of effort and/or low scores on the filler items (n = 3); • Incomplete data sets (n = 4).
Demographic details of the included participants are provided in Table 1.
table.formatted: Demographic details of the included participants are provided in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

table.text: Materials Participants completed a contextualized acceptability judgement task (AJT) testing acceptance of MECs in two conditions: five verb types (have, give, build, find, want) and six questions words (what, who, where, when, how, why).
All participants completed one list in English, and the L2 English learners completed another list in their L1.
Results for control and filler items are not discussed in what follows because participants were required to be target-like for inclusion.
Regarding the L2 English Interlanguage grammar, we found residual evidence of transfer, though our participants were sufficiently advanced that they were approaching target-like behavior.
One might also seek participants with lower L2 English proficiency than the participants recruited for the present study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Participants completed an acceptability judgement task that tested for the presence of MECs in their English Interlanguage system with a focus on the two implicational hierarchies presented above: (1) verb-type, and (2) question word.
Participants were recruited via Prolific and provided with $10 compensation for their time.
At the time of testing, participants were living in the United States (L1 English), Spain (L1 Spanish), or France (L1 French).
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old.

Participants were excluded for one or more of the following reasons: • Simultaneous bilinguals and/or English not the L2 (n = 3); • Clear lack of effort and/or low scores on the filler items (n = 3); • Incomplete data sets (n = 4).
Demographic details of the included participants are provided in Table 1.

Materials Participants completed a contextualized acceptability judgement task (AJT) testing acceptance of MECs in two conditions: five verb types (have, give, build, find, want) and six questions words (what, who, where, when, how, why).
All participants completed one list in English, and the L2 English learners completed another list in their L1.
Results for control and filler items are not discussed in what follows because participants were required to be target-like for inclusion.
Regarding the L2 English Interlanguage grammar, we found residual evidence of transfer, though our participants were sufficiently advanced that they were approaching target-like behavior.
One might also seek participants with lower L2 English proficiency than the participants recruited for the present study.

info.title: Unlearning Modal Existential Constructions in L2 English Implicational Universals and Frequency

text.text: For many years, the problem of preemption has been discussed in second language acquisition research, i.e., how a learner 'unlearns' an initially transferred representation when the input does not provide contradictory evidence.
In this study we examine how Yang's (2002) Variational Learning model can account for cases of preemption.
To do so, we address the expungement of Modal Existential Constructions (MECs) from the L2 English Interlanguage grammar of L1 Spanish and French learners.
Using an acceptability judgement task, we analyze participants' retreat from non-facilitative transfer considering two implicational universals associated with MECs and frequency effects.
We find that the more marked an element is on an implicational hierarchy, the easier it is to remove.
However, there is also evidence that frequency interacts with markedness to affect the rate of restructuring.

These findings suggest a need to more seriously consider how domainspecific (language universals) and domain-general learning mechanisms (frequency) interact during second language acquisition and grammar restructuring.

To successfully acquire a second language (L2), one must not only learn new sounds, vocabulary, and grammatical regularities, but also unlearn a great deal of linguistic baggage from one's native language (e.g., Trahey & White, 1993; White, 2003).
text.formatted: To successfully acquire a second language (L2), one must not only learn new sounds, vocabulary, and grammatical regularities, but also unlearn a great deal of linguistic baggage from one's native language (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Trahey & White, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">White, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, this preemption problem may seem particularly acute when one's native language (L1) provides two options, while the target language allows one but not the other.

This is because there is no direct negative evidence in the primary linguistic data of the new language that directly indicates that only one of the options available in one's native language is well-formed in the new language.

For example, in contexts of circumstantial possibility, Spanish and French (among many other languages) allow the use of both an indefinite pronoun and a Modal Existential Construction (MEC), while English allows only the former.
Therefore, because L1 Spanish and L1 French learners of L2 English may initially transfer the availability of both options, in acquiring English they will need to preempt the availability of the MEC.
This unlearning presents a learnability issue, however, due to their low frequency of occurrence and the lack of negative evidence in the input.
This study investigates the extent to which Yang's (2002) Variational Learning model (VL) can provide insights into the preemption of the MEC by L1 Spanish and L1 French learners of English.
text.formatted: This study investigates the extent to which <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Yang's (2002)</ref> Variational Learning model (VL) can provide insights into the preemption of the MEC by L1 Spanish and L1 French learners of English.

text.text: While there is no (positive) evidence in the input that shows that the MEC is ungrammatical in English, VL raises the possibility that overcoming the preemption problem may occur through competition between multiple grammars.

Furthermore, the interaction of frequency effects with an implicational universal (presumably, a part of Universal Grammar) may shed light on both the transfer of MECs from the L1 and the path toward their expungement in L2 English.
We implement an acceptability judgement task, testing acceptance of MECs along two implicational hierarchies: MEC-embedding verbs and wh-words that may occur in MECs.

Linguists have long been fascinated by what Baker and McCarthy (1981) termed "the logical problem of language acquisition": learners must project an infinite range of grammatical expressions despite exposure to only a finite set of primary linguistic data.
text.formatted: Linguists have long been fascinated by what <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Baker and McCarthy (1981)</ref> termed "the logical problem of language acquisition": learners must project an infinite range of grammatical expressions despite exposure to only a finite set of primary linguistic data.

text.text: That is, the task of language acquisition is underdetermined by the data available to the learner, which would pose challenges for the acquirer if their only resource were the language input (Hornstein & Lightfoot, 1981; White, 2003).
text.formatted: That is, the task of language acquisition is underdetermined by the data available to the learner, which would pose challenges for the acquirer if their only resource were the language input <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hornstein & Lightfoot, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">White, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: As such, (some) researchers have postulated various types of constraints on the acquirer's available hypothesis space (in the tradition of Chomsky, 1965).
text.formatted: As such, (some) researchers have postulated various types of constraints on the acquirer's available hypothesis space (in the tradition of <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Chomsky, 1965)</ref>.

text.text: We will not review the various approaches to such constraints here.

Instead, we will focus on one model of language acquisition: VL provides a formal means of integrating the quantitative properties of the input with constraints on the possible grammars an acquirer will postulate (Yang, 2002; Legate & Yang, 2007).
text.formatted: Instead, we will focus on one model of language acquisition: VL provides a formal means of integrating the quantitative properties of the input with constraints on the possible grammars an acquirer will postulate <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Yang, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Legate & Yang, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Under VL, the learner posits a population of competing grammars which is constrained by the innate hypothesis space given by UG.

Within this hypothesis space, grammars are probabilistically selected to parse the input, and the success (or failure) of the chosen grammar then affects the probability that it will be selected again in the future.
The algorithm in (1) illustrates this process (Yang, 2002, pp. 26-27).
text.formatted: The algorithm in (1) illustrates this process <ref type="bibr">(Yang, 2002, pp. 26-27)</ref>.

text.text: (1) Upon the presentation of an input datum s, the child a. selects a grammar Gi with probability Pi b. analyzes s with Gi c. if successful, reward Gi by increasing Pi otherwise, punish Gi by decreasing Pi Thus, convergence on the target grammar is determined by the interaction of language universals (provided by UG), which constrain the hypothesis space, and input frequency (quantitative properties of the input), which provides evidence of the relative strengths of each posited grammar in the target language.
While VL was developed for L1 acquisition, it can be extended to L2 acquisition as well, with some key differences.

While the initial state of L1 acquisition is essentially just the constraints placed on the available hypothesis space, we assume the initial state of L2 acquisition to be the steady state of the L1 system (Schwartz & Sprouse, 1996).
text.formatted: While the initial state of L1 acquisition is essentially just the constraints placed on the available hypothesis space, we assume the initial state of L2 acquisition to be the steady state of the L1 system <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Schwartz & Sprouse, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Under a VL account, the L2 initial state is therefore the L1 probabilities that particular grammars are chosen.
If the L2 input is not consistent with the transferred system, the probabilities of particular grammars being chosen must be adjusted.
Some researchers also suggest the L1 grammar may retain a privileged or default role (Slabakova, 2008; Yang & Montrul, 2017).
text.formatted: Some researchers also suggest the L1 grammar may retain a privileged or default role <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Slabakova, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Yang & Montrul, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the speed of restructuring from previous non-facilitative transfer (i.e., convergence on the target grammar) is dependent on the target language input, including frequency of the kind of input necessary for prompting changes to the current state of probabilities.

Of course, frequency of input in the L2 is often qualitatively and quantitatively different from that of the L1, and many additional factors not relevant in L1 acquisition play a role in the learner's convergence on the target grammar, such as variability in learner-directed speech, settings in which input is received, type of input (written vs. oral), and individual differences in language learning aptitude. 1Given our goal in this paper of applying VL to L2 acquisition research, we now discuss findings in L2 regarding its two components: frequency (quantitative properties) and implicational universals (constraints on the hypothesis space).
text.formatted: Of course, frequency of input in the L2 is often qualitatively and quantitatively different from that of the L1, and many additional factors not relevant in L1 acquisition play a role in the learner's convergence on the target grammar, such as variability in learner-directed speech, settings in which input is received, type of input (written vs. oral), and individual differences in language learning aptitude. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref>Given our goal in this paper of applying VL to L2 acquisition research, we now discuss findings in L2 regarding its two components: frequency (quantitative properties) and implicational universals (constraints on the hypothesis space).

text.text: First, researchers across all traditions generally agree that input is vital for L2 acquisition (Rankin & Unsworth, 2016; Slabakova et al., 2014).
text.formatted: First, researchers across all traditions generally agree that input is vital for L2 acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Rankin & Unsworth, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Slabakova et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, while usage-based accounts (e.g., Wulff & Ellis, 2018; Tomasello, 2003) attempt to demonstrate that (second) language acquisition can be accomplished solely through the use of domain-general cognition and data-driven learning, generative accounts attribute an additional important role to domain-specific cognitive principles and/or mechanisms which constrain the acquisition process (Schwartz & Sprouse, 2013 , 2026; White, 2003).
text.formatted: However, while usage-based accounts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Wulff & Ellis, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Tomasello, 2003)</ref> attempt to demonstrate that (second) language acquisition can be accomplished solely through the use of domain-general cognition and data-driven learning, generative accounts attribute an additional important role to domain-specific cognitive principles and/or mechanisms which constrain the acquisition process <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Schwartz & Sprouse, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">White, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, VL is more aligned with these latter accounts.

Researchers in the generative tradition typically point to two findings in discussing the role of frequency in L2 acquisition: non-acquisition despite frequent input and acquisition despite a poverty of the stimulus.
On the first point, consider suppliance of obligatory morphology, such as third person singular present tense -s in English.

While such morphology is exorbitantly frequent in the input, no matter how frequency is calculated, and taught/corrected extensively in class, even highly proficient learners of English whose L1s exhibit subject-verb agreement morphology may still not supply correct morphology in production (e.g., VanPatten et al., 2012; VanPatten & Williams, 2014).

In comparison to English, Spanish displays much more abundant evidence for subject agreement, and under VL, one would predict a faster rate of acquisition of the target property when evidence is more frequent.
As predicted, the L2 Spanish acquirers displayed higher accuracy in comprehending agreement than the L2 English acquirers.
So, to date, research applying VL to L2 acquisition has been promising, but it has focused only on its first component, frequency.
Of course, many studies have addressed constraints on the hypothesis space with L2 (i.e., universals), but separately from the framework of VL.
Therefore, L2 VL studies have not yet addressed the role of implicational universals, or universals generally, in interaction with the role of frequency.
Finally, VL has not been tested on the acquisition of properties at the lexicon-syntax interface in L2.
The goal of this paper is to undertake such an investigation.
In numerous languages, there exists a phenomenon called the modal existential (wh-)construction (MEC; Grosu, 2004; Šimík, 2011), illustrated in (2)-(3) below.

text.text: MECs exhibit three core components.
First, they belong to the class of wh-constructions, such as wh-questions and free relatives.
That is, MECs obligatorily contain a wh-word that must be fronted, so only languages that have overt wh-movement may exhibit MECs.
However, even in languages with overt wh-movement, MECs may not exist; for example, Romance languages display MECs (2-3), but (most) Germanic languages do not (4).

Second, MECs belong to the class of existential constructions, such as there-existential sentences in English.
That is, MECs always assert the existence of something, and they are typically embedded under existential predicates (e.g., be or have).
Finally, they belong to the class of modal constructions, such as infinitives embedded under modal verbs or infinitival relative clauses.
Specifically, MECs always display a circumstantial possibility reading, never carrying deontic/epistemic flavors or necessity force.
Šimík (2011) identifies four implicational universals associated with MECs, alongside four absolute universals and five tendencies.
Here, we focus on two of the implicational universals.
The first of these involves the set of verbs that embed MECs (5).
The least marked verbs are those that are typically used in existential constructions cross-linguistically, such as be and have (have-type).
More marked are dynamic predicates, such as find and seek (find-type), give and bring (give-type), and build and buy (build-type).
Thus, the verbs that can embed MECs are those whose lexical meaning supports existential quantification of an indefinite internal argument (Szabolcsi, 1986; Grosu, 2004).

text.text: Notably, however, verbs such as want and need (want-type) cannot embed MECs.

This study investigates the transfer of MECs by L1 Spanish and L1 French learners to L2 English, as well as the subsequent restructuring of the L2 Interlanguage grammar (retreat from transfer), through the lens of VL.

Participants completed an acceptability judgement task that tested for the presence of MECs in their English Interlanguage system with a focus on the two implicational hierarchies presented above: (1) verb-type, and (2) question word.
The research questions underlying this study are as follows: 1.
Do learners transfer MECs?
Guided by Schwartz and Sprouse's (1996) assumptions of full transfer of the L1 system at the onset of L2 acquisition, we first sought to verify whether MECs transfer from the L1 to the L2.
text.formatted: Guided by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Schwartz and Sprouse's (1996)</ref> assumptions of full transfer of the L1 system at the onset of L2 acquisition, we first sought to verify whether MECs transfer from the L1 to the L2.

text.text: However, the granularity of said transfer is still unclear.

That is, will learners transfer the licensing of MECs generally, or will precisely the lexical items (verbs and/or wh-words) that occur with MECs in the L1 be the only lexical items that occur with MECs in the L2?
Sprouse's (2006) Relexification Hypothesis predicts the latter.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Sprouse's (2006)</ref> Relexification Hypothesis predicts the latter.

text.text: Do the implicational universals associated with MECs determine the path in which learners retreat from transfer?
Following VL, the implicational universals will determine the path in which learners retreat from transfer.
Specifically, if the implicational universals play a role, learners should retreat from the more marked grammar either before, or simultaneously with, the less marked grammar.
How does input frequency interact with any effect found for the role of implicational universals?
While it would be fully consistent with VL that input frequency interacts with implicational universals in the case of MECs, VL does not necessarily require this.
Participants Data were collected from 25 L1 English, 33 L1 Spanish/L2 English, and 32 L1 French/L2 English participants.
Participants were recruited via Prolific and provided with $10 compensation for their time.
At the time of testing, participants were living in the United States (L1 English), Spain (L1 Spanish), or France (L1 French).
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old.

Additionally, the L2 English groups were required to have acquired English as their L2 sensu stricto, i.e., as the first language after their L1, but they were not restricted regarding further sequentially acquired languages.
Simultaneous bilinguals (multiple L1s) were not included.
The L1 English group was not restricted regarding languages acquired sequentially after the L1 (i.e., L2+), but as with the L2 groups, simultaneous bilinguals were excluded.
Of the recruited participants, 8 were later excluded from the analysis.
Because the study was conducted remotely and due to our recruitment method, more conservative attention to the data was adopted.

Participants were excluded for one or more of the following reasons: • Simultaneous bilinguals and/or English not the L2 (n = 3); • Clear lack of effort and/or low scores on the filler items (n = 3); • Incomplete data sets (n = 4).

These conditions were not fully crossed, however, because appropriate context/sentence pairs could not be created for all verb/question pairs (e.g., 'John built someone...').

In this study we examined the preemption of MECs by L1 Spanish and L1 French learners of L2 English.
We first examined the learners' behavior in their L1s, finding that while the L1 Spanish learners behaved as expected, based on the extant literature, the L1 French learners did not.
That is, the L1 Spanish learners accepted MECs with all (licit) embedding verbs and with all wh-words.
The L1 French learners, however, accepted MECs with all (licit) embedding verbs (as expected), but only rejected MECs with why, accepting all other wh-words (contra Hirschbühler, 1978).
text.formatted: The L1 French learners, however, accepted MECs with all (licit) embedding verbs (as expected), but only rejected MECs with why, accepting all other wh-words <ref type="bibr">(contra Hirschbühler, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: We also found that the L1 English speakers performed largely as expected in English: generally rejecting MECs regardless of the wh-word or the embedding verb.
However, there was some increased acceptance of find-type verbs.
We suggest that this behavior is due to many of the items containing these verbs being grammatical strings, albeit not appropriate in the provided context.
Regarding the L2 English Interlanguage grammar, we found residual evidence of transfer, though our participants were sufficiently advanced that they were approaching target-like behavior.
Further evidence of transfer was found in the effects of proficiency on participants' ratings (i.e., ratings were higher at lower proficiencies).
Additionally, both groups tended to rate MECs with find-type verbs higher than other verb-types.
Again, this behavior may be linked to a lack of integration of the context when making the acceptability judgement.
Furthermore, for the L1 Spanish learners, who were generally more accepting of MECs, there was a trend for have-type verbs to be rated higher than other verb types.
This trend suggests that preempting less marked options in an implicational universal is more difficult than preempting more marked options.
Furthermore, we found that, among the wh-words, why (the most marked wh-word) was typically rated lower than the others.
Again, this behavior points to markedness within an implicational hierarchy playing a role in the ease of preemption.
Finally, where tended to be rated higher than the other wh-words by both groups.
We address this finding in the following section.

To get a sense of the occurrence of each wh-word in MECs cross-linguistically, we searched the Spanish Web 2023 (esTenTen) corpus, which is a corpus of collected internet texts from European and American Spanish, using SketchEngine (Kilgarriff & Renau, 2013).

text.text: We employed a CQL search consisting of the lemma tener ('to have'), an optional preposition, a wh-word, and an infinitive verb, and the returned tokens were manually checked by a native Spanish speaker to remove sentences that were not MECs.
We found that about 60 percent of all the identified MECs contained 'what' and 'who', but only about 15 percent contained 'where'.
The remaining 25 percent of MECs were distributed among the other wh-words.

These findings correspond to Šimík's (2008) corpus search of Czech MECs, where 'what' and 'who' accounted for 44 and 34 percent of all MECs found, respectively; 22 percent contained 'when', 'how', and 'why' combined.

Next, to get a sense of the type and amount of (relevant) input the L2 learners would be exposed to in English, we searched for contexts where MECs would be licit in the L1.
We used simple string searches consisting of the verb have (lemma), some-/any-indefinites, and to (e.g., 'have something to').
The returned tokens were further manually checked to remove any tokens that would not allow MECs in Spanish or French.
For example, 'I can't come, I have something do' would be removed because it has the incorrect modal flavor (i.e., deontic) and force (i.e., necessity).
We only conducted the search for the indefinite pronouns corresponding to 'what', 'who', and 'where' because the other wh-words do not have indefinite pronouns of the same type (e.g., *somewhen).

However, based on the findings from our search of the L1 Spanish corpus and Šimík's (2008) Czech corpus search, we expect that the contexts that would allow MECs with 'when', 'how', and 'why' would occur less frequently in the English input as well.

text.text: While there are a few examples of MEC-licit contexts in two of the L2 corpora, there are none in the third.
Additionally, their occurrence per million words is not particularly high even in the BNC.
Still, a pattern starts to emerge among the three searched indefinites: contexts where 'what'-MECs would be licit occur most frequently, followed by 'who'-MECs, and 'where'-MECs are least frequent.
In fact, across all the L2 corpora, no instances of contexts where a 'where'-MEC would be licit in the L1 were found.
We assume that the choice between the MEC and the indefinite pronoun is in competition under VL.

As the learner continues to encounter input that can be successfully parsed with the indefinite pronoun, but never encounters input that rewards the MEC grammar, the probability of selecting the grammar with the indefinite pronoun increases.

Because the combined probability of selecting either grammar can never exceed 1.0, the probability of selecting the grammar with the MEC correspondingly decreases with each increase for the indefinite pronoun grammar.
This process continues until the probability of selecting the MEC grammar is at such a negligible level that it is never retrieved or difficult to access.
Functionally, at this point the MEC grammar has been expunged/preempted from the interlanguage system.

We would therefore expect that MECs with wh-words where the corresponding combination of an MEC embedding verb and the indefinite pronoun (e.g., have what vs. have something) are less frequent in the input will be expunged more slowly because the rewards for the indefinite pronoun grammar are accruing at a slower rate.
Note that this argumentation assumes that the granularity of competing grammars is at the lexical level and not simply broad constructions.
Therefore, based on the corpus findings above, MECs occurring with 'where', 'how', 'when', and 'why' should be expunged more slowly than MECs occurring with 'what' or 'who'.
However, it is at this point that the implicational universals play a role.
Because the whwords other than 'where' are lower (more marked) in the hierarchy, they must be expunged when something higher (less marked) on the hierarchy is expunged.
So, as the high frequency of occurrence for 'what' and 'who' MECs leads to their preemption, it also causes the preemption of 'when', 'how', and 'why' MECs.
However, because 'where' is at the same level of the implicational hierarchy as 'what' and 'who', its preemption is not caused by their expungement.
This is exactly the pattern observed for the L1 Spanish learners.
To wrap up our discussion, we return to our three research questions.
RQ 1: Do learners transfer MECs?

Yes, but we were unable to delve into Sprouse's (2006) fine-grained Relexification Hypothesis as planned, because our L1 French data do not match the claimed difference in acceptability of MECs with different wh-words.
RQ 2: Do the implicational universals associated with MECs determine the path in which learners retreat from transfer?
Yes, it seems that wh-words on the more marked end of the hierarchy are easier to expunge from the Interlanguage grammar than those at the less marked end of the hierarchy.
RQ 3: How does input frequency interact with any effect found for the role of implicational universals?
We were able to observe this effect only for the interaction with the implicational universal regarding wh-words, but not for the implicational universal regarding embedding predicates.
In this case, the preemption of less marked (but more frequently occurring) wh-words caused the preemption of more marked (but less frequent) wh-words.
However, the preemption of the more frequent wh-words did not cause the preemption of less frequent wh-words at the same level of markedness.

This study focused on one of the under-investigated puzzles of nonnative language acquisition, viz., how it is possible for a developing Interlanguage grammar to retreat from a morphosyntactic possibility transferred from the L1 when there is no direct negative evidence in the TL input that the structure in question is ungrammatical in the L2.

In the case at hand, the poverty of the stimulus for the retraction is particularly acute for (at least) three reasons: (1) The transferred structure is associated with a subtle semantic effect (circumstantial possibility, not deontic or epistemic modality).
(2) The unacceptability of the transferred structure is not mentioned in language instruction.

(3) Discourse contexts in which either the ungrammatical L1 structure or its grammatical L2 paraphrase might occur appear to be strikingly infrequent. Yang's (2002) Variational Learning approach, nevertheless, offers a way to model the observable differences between L1 Spanish vs.

First, there is clear evidence in their acceptability ratings that learners in both groups have transferred the possibility of MECs from their L1, given that there is nothing in the L2 input to suggest that MECs are licit in English.

Furthermore, the L1 Spanish learners display an overall higher rate of acceptance of MECs in English than the L1 French learners do, aligning with the fact that MECs are generally rated lower in L1 French than in L1 Spanish.

Assuming that in contexts of circumstantial possibility there is a competition between an MEC and an indefinite pronoun, the contexts in which an MEC are headed by 'where' appear to be less frequent, and thus MECs with 'where' are slower to be expunged than MECs with 'what' and 'who.'
This confirms the relevance of frequency in the sense of VL.

This study is limited specifically because it examines the retraction from a transferred structure for which there are very infrequent discourse contexts for competition, and the level of granularity of our results cannot fully match those found in the syntax-semantics literature based on introspective data from L1 speakers of languages that sanction MECs.
Furthermore, it would be impractical to conduct longitudinal studies tracking the retreat from MECs in the English Interlanguage grammars of individual learners.
Thus, we have had to rely on relatively crude measures such as self-reported language dominance.
Nevertheless, an overall picture has emerged that is consistent with expectations derived from Yang's VL approach.

Additionally, our experimental results for French do not fully match what is reported in the syntax-semantics literature (e.g., Hirschbühler 1978; Šimik 2011); thus, we could not test the granularity of transfer at the level of individual lexical items (in the sense of Sprouse 2006).

text.text: Finally, this study considered L2 learners whose L1s differ in the set of wh-words that may be used in MECs.
Future research could investigate L2 learners whose L1s differ in the set of verbs that can embed MECs or that differ in both respects.
One might also seek participants with lower L2 English proficiency than the participants recruited for the present study.
This would allow for a more nuanced investigation of the granularity of transfer.
On a broader scale, further research could consider other cases of potential interaction of frequency with implicational universals.
